title: 3D Shape & Space
description: Describe and combine three-dimensional shapes in ray-marched space.

lessons.title: Box and torus SDFs
lessons.intro: A sphere is the one solid whose distance function needs no thought, because length already measures it and does not care how many components it was handed. Everything else has to be constructed, and the two shapes here are constructed by quite different tricks. A box comes from folding space with abs so that only one corner of it has to be reasoned about, then measuring how far past that corner you are. A torus comes from taking a distance you have already worked out and using it as a coordinate for a second one. Both are three lines long, both are exact everywhere, and both are still Module 3's operators with one more component along for the ride.
lessons.takeaway: abs folds all eight octants onto one, so a box need only be measured in a single corner. q is how far past the box you are on each axis; length(max(q, 0.0)) is the exact distance for a point outside, since the negative components are flattened to zero and drop out of the length, and min(max(q.x, max(q.y, q.z)), 0.0) supplies the inside distance the first term cannot, because inside every component of q is negative and the largest of them names the nearest face. sdTorus is a distance built from a distance: length(p.xz) minus the major radius says how far you are from the ring's circle, and that pairs with p.y into a two-dimensional offset whose length, less the tube radius, is the answer. min unites two of them, unchanged from Module 3.
lessons.tryThis: Raise the torus's tube radius in the third stage from 0.3 to 0.8, the same as its major radius, and work out what becomes of the hole before you look at it. Then swap min for max in the last stage and say why the picture goes entirely dark, with not one lit pixel left.

stages.title: abs folds space into one corner
stages.body: abs(p) reflects every octant of space onto the one where all three components are positive, so a box centred on the origin only has to be measured once, in that corner. q is what is left after subtracting the half-extents: how far past the box you are on each axis, negative where you are still inside it. At the box's own centre q is minus 0.6, minus 0.45, minus 0.6; max of that against zero is nothing at all, so the first term contributes nothing, and the second returns minus 0.45, the distance to the nearest face. Step 0.3 beyond one face and q's first component becomes 0.3 while the other two stay negative, so the length is 0.3 and the second term clamps away. Step past two faces at once and q is 0.3, 0.3, minus 0.6, whose positive part has length 0.4243 — the true diagonal distance to the edge, which no single axis could have given. The render is an exact rectangle, because a box seen straight down its own axis is one: 0.6 and 0.45 over the near face's depth of 2.4, times the focal length of 1.5, gives half-extents of 0.375 and 0.28125, and the march reports 0.3756 and 0.2818, the extra thousandth in each being the hit threshold. That is 28.2 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges, and on a preview between 1.4 and 2.4 times as wide as it is tall it sits well clear of the sides at every width. Every hit lands on the single front face: t runs 2.400 dead ahead and 2.514 at the corners, and all of that spread is the rays fanning out rather than the surface receding.

stages.title: Subtract a radius
stages.body: Subtracting a constant from any distance field moves its zero surface outward by that much in every direction at once, and on a box that means the flats move out and the edges become quarter-cylinders. Shrinking the half-extents by the same amount first is what keeps the overall size fixed, so the solid still reaches 0.6, 0.45 and 0.6 whatever r is doing. Here r sweeps from 0 to 0.30 and back every 10.47 seconds, and at the bottom of that sweep the render is the previous stage exactly, since subtracting nothing from a box shrunk by nothing is the box. What the rounding costs is not spread evenly. Straight out sideways the silhouette falls from 0.3756 to 0.3387, 9.82 per cent; straight up it falls from 0.2818 to 0.2537, 9.98 per cent; but measured out along the 45-degree diagonal it falls from 0.3986 to 0.3379, 15.23 per cent. The 0.3986 is worth pausing on: with sharp edges it is exactly the square root of two times the half-height, which is what having a corner there means. At the top of the sweep the flat part of the front face is only 0.6 by 0.3 in world units and everything outside that is fillet, which is why the corner gives up half as much again as the flats do.

stages.title: A distance from a distance
stages.body: length(p.xz) minus the major radius is Module 3's circle, computed in the plane the ring lies in: it says how far you are from the ring's centre line, positive outside and negative inside. That number is not the answer, it is a coordinate. Pair it with p.y and you have a two-dimensional offset from the nearest point of the ring, and the length of that, less the tube radius, is the distance to the surface. Two circles, one nested inside the other. The swizzle q.xzy hands sdTorus the point with its y and z traded, which stands the ring up so its hole faces the camera. With a major radius of 0.8 and a tube of 0.3 at three units out, the render is a true annulus — the same on every traverse, because the ring is symmetric about the view axis — with an outer edge at 0.5611 and an inner edge at 0.2471 in p units. Geometry agrees: the ring's centre line sits at atan of 0.8 over 3, which is 14.931 degrees, and the tube subtends asin of 0.3 over 3.1048, which is 5.545 degrees, so the two edges should fall at 0.5601 and 0.2480. Each is out by about a thousandth, in the direction the hit threshold pushes them, and the solid is fatter on both sides. The hole is genuinely empty: on the axis sdTorus returns 0.8 minus 0.3, a clear half a unit, so the centre ray never converges on anything and leaves past 20. The outer edge reaches 56.1 per cent of the way to the top and bottom edges.

stages.title: Both, with min
stages.body: min over two fields is the union, and it does not care that the fields describe different kinds of shape or that one lies inside the other's hole. The bar is a box with half-extents of 0.2, 0.2 and 1.0, so it runs from z of 2 to z of 4 and passes clean through the ring. A flat fill would not be able to say which of them is in front, so this stage spends t instead, mixing between the two colours across a smoothstep from 2.0 to 4.0. The bar's near face sits at 2.0, and 1.5 times 0.2 over 2.0 puts its silhouette at exactly 0.15 in p units with corners at 0.2121; the march gives 0.1508 and 0.2129. Those corners reach 0.2828 in world units across the ring's plane, against a hole 0.5 wide, so the two solids never touch — and background shows all the way round between them, a band 0.0961 wide in p units straight out along the two screen axes, narrowing to 0.0338 out at 45 degrees where the bar's corners come nearest the ring's inner edge. The colours say the rest. The bar's front face is flat, running from t of 2.000 to 2.020 across its whole width, so it comes back at very nearly the undiluted near colour, 0.780, 0.960, 0.390. The ring is further and reads it. At the nose of its tube t is 2.805 and the colour 0.567, 0.768, 0.447. Both rims are further than that and identical to each other, which is forced rather than lucky: the silhouette ray on the inside of the ring and the one on the outside are tangent to the same circular cross-section of the tube, and the two tangent lengths from a point to a circle are equal, so each of them sits at a t of 3.0903 and a colour of 0.439, 0.654, 0.481. That is a limit approached rather than reached, since a ray exactly on a tangent grazes for ever, so the outermost pixels that do converge stop short of it on either side, neither of them arriving.

lessons.title: Smooth minimum
lessons.intro: min is the correct answer to a question slightly narrower than the one being asked. It returns the distance to whichever surface is nearer, which is exactly what a union needs and exactly why a union built from min has a hard corner wherever the two surfaces cross: at that crossing the field stops following one shape and starts following the other in an instant, and a field with a kink in it has a kink on its zero surface too. A smooth minimum is min with that switch smeared out over a width you choose. It is one clamp, one mix and one correction term, and past a certain width it does something min can never do.
lessons.takeaway: smin interpolates between the two distances rather than picking one. h is where the two stand relative to each other, scaled by k and clamped, so once they differ by more than k it saturates and smin returns exactly what min would — which is why blending never disturbs the parts of a shape away from the join. The correction term k times h times one minus h peaks at a quarter of k in the middle, so where the two distances are equal the field is pushed down by k over 4 and the surface moves outward to meet the new zero. k is measured in world units, not screen units, and a k large enough will weld together two shapes that never touch at all.
lessons.tryThis: In the third stage, work out from the field alone how far the waist should sit above the sphere centres when k is 0.5, then check it against what renders. In the last stage, move the spheres to plus and minus 0.6 and predict the new k at which the weld appears before you change anything else.

stages.title: The corner min leaves
stages.body: Two spheres of radius 0.5, centred 0.44 either side of the axis and three units out. Their centres are 0.88 apart and their radii sum to 1.0, so they overlap, and the circle where the two surfaces cross has a radius of 0.2375 in world units. min unites them into one solid, and the outline shows precisely where the union was welded and where it was not. The two ends are untouched: the silhouette reaches 0.4841 in p units either side, and the tallest point of each lobe is 0.2550, out at p.x of 0.2263. On the vertical centre line, though, the outline pinches to 0.1220 — 47.9 per cent of the lobe height — and it does not curve into that pinch, it turns a corner. Projecting the intersection circle puts that corner at 0.1191, and the 0.0029 of difference is the hit threshold, which costs more at a corner than anywhere else: a ray creeping past a sharp edge stays within a thousandth of it for a stretch rather than an instant. Tighten the threshold from 0.001 to 0.00001 and the rendered waist walks back to 0.11913, against the 0.11912 the geometry asks for. The corner is not only in the outline. It runs across the surface as a ridge from the top notch to the bottom one; the outline is that same ridge seen edge-on, which is the only part of it a flat fill can show.

stages.title: smin welds it
stages.body: The same two spheres, with min replaced by smin at a k of 0.3, and the corner is gone. The waist rises from 0.1220 to 0.1890 in p units, and nothing else on screen moves: the ends stand at 0.484140 with min and 0.484150 with the blend, a difference of one hundred-thousandth, and the tallest point of each lobe stays at 0.2550. That is not luck, it is the clamp. At the right-hand end the near sphere's distance is 0 and the far one's is 0.88; 0.88 is far more than k, so h pins to one end of its range, the correction term collapses to nothing, and smin returns exactly what min returned. The blend can only act where the two distances are within k of each other. Where they are equal it acts hardest, because k times h times one minus h is largest at h of a half, giving k over 4 — here 0.075. So on the vertical centre line the field reads 0.075 less than it did, and the surface moves out to where the old field was 0.075: solving that puts the waist's world half-height at 0.3702 instead of 0.2375. At three units out the camera turns one world unit into half a unit of p, so that 0.1327 of world becomes 0.0663 on screen — against the 0.0670 the render actually moves, the remainder being the same threshold that widened the corner in the last stage.

stages.title: k is the control
stages.body: k is an argument now, sweeping from 0.02 to 0.50 and back every 12.57 seconds, and what it moves is worth watching against what it leaves alone. The waist climbs steadily: 0.1272 at the bottom of the sweep, 0.1465 at k of 0.10, 0.1685 at 0.20, 0.1890 at 0.30, 0.2083 at 0.40 and 0.2269 at the top, against 0.1220 for the plain min of the first stage. Over the whole sweep the two ends move from 0.484140 to 0.484155 and the lobes stay 0.2550 tall to four decimal places. The entire effect is confined to the join, and the reason is arithmetic rather than taste: away from the join the two distances differ by much more than k, h saturates, and smin is min. Note that k is not a screen measurement. It is a world distance, and at this depth the camera turns one world unit into half a unit of p. What the blend spends is not k either but k over 4, the height of the correction term: at the top of the sweep that is 0.125 of world, whose straight projection would be 0.0625 of p, and yet the waist has risen 0.1049 above where min left it. A surface moves by its field's drop divided by how steeply that field was climbing, and between two nearly opposed surfaces it climbs slowly, so the same drop buys more travel there than it would anywhere else.

stages.title: A shape that needs the blend
stages.body: These two spheres do not touch. Radius 0.42, centred 0.5 either side of the axis, so their surfaces face each other across a gap of 0.16 and no amount of min will ever join them: min would give two discs for ever, with inner edges at plus and minus 0.0399 by geometry and 0.0388 as rendered, leaving a strip of background 0.0775 wide down the middle. smin can join them, and exactly when it does is predictable. At the midpoint both distances are 0.08, which is the case where smin returns the distance minus k over 4, so the field there is 0.08 minus a quarter of k and it reaches zero at k of 0.32 precisely. Below that the strip merely narrows — 0.0388 of p either side of the axis at a k of 0.05, still 0.0131 at 0.30 — and above it there is a weld, reaching 0.0262 above the axis right at the threshold, 0.0765 at k of 0.40, 0.1124 at 0.50 and 0.1407 at 0.60. k sweeps 0.05 to 0.60 every 12.57 seconds, so by the arithmetic the two are one shape for 6.36 of those seconds and two for the rest. What gets drawn runs longer, and not merely because a field within 0.001 of zero counts as solid. Near the onset the field along the axis is so nearly flat that the march spends all sixty-four of its steps without ever converging, and since the t it hands back is still under 20, the fill paints it solid anyway. That lights the middle of the frame at a k of 0.3082 on the narrowest preview and the widest alike, stretching the joined part of the cycle to 6.53 seconds; a preview an odd number of pixels across sits its columns half a pixel over, lights at 0.3095, and gets 6.51. Through all of it the lobes are untouched, reaching 0.4714 either side and 0.2133 above and below at every k in the sweep.

lessons.title: Repetition and transforms in 3D
lessons.intro: Every scene so far has held as many shapes as its map function had lines. Repetition breaks that relationship. Take the point the ray has reached, keep only where it sits inside a cell of a grid, and hand that to a single sphere: the same three lines now describe a lattice running away for ever in all three directions, and it costs what one sphere cost. Module 5 did this on a flat plane with a shape that was drawn rather than marched, so a wrong answer merely looked odd. Here the same arithmetic feeds a loop that trusts every number it is given, and the first stage is what that trust buys when the arithmetic is careless.
lessons.takeaway: fract(p) is the position within a unit cell measured from the cell's low corner, so a shape written around the origin lands on that corner and is cut into eighths — and worse, the value jumps at every wall, which stops the result being a distance field at all. Subtracting a half puts the shape in the middle of its cell, and for a sphere that field is not merely usable but exact, because the nearest centre is the nearest one on each axis taken separately. floor(p) is the cell's id, constant everywhere inside the cell, so anything derived from it varies between copies and never within one. A rotation applied to the cell coordinate turns each copy where it stands, and since a rotation preserves length it costs the field nothing.
lessons.tryThis: Change the 0.5 in the second stage to 0.25 and work out which way every sphere moves and whether any of them now crosses a cell wall, before you look. Then set the box half-extent in the last stage from 0.22 to 0.4 and say what the 0.3111 figure predicts will go wrong.

stages.title: fract, and what it costs
stages.body: fract runs 0 to 1 on each axis, so the point handed to sdSphere is measured from the low corner of whichever cell the ray is in, and a sphere written around the origin therefore sits on that corner. Only the eighth of it with all three components positive is inside the cell, so what this field actually describes is an eighth-sphere at every whole-numbered point in space. The geometry is the smaller of the two problems. Cross a cell wall and fract falls from just under one to zero, which drops the reported distance from as much as 1.4321 to minus 0.3 across no distance at all. That is not a distance field, it is a function that happens to be zero on a surface, and the march believes it: a ray told it may safely travel 1.4321 travels 1.4321, straight through whatever was 0.001 ahead. Counted pixel by pixel when the camera passes a whole-numbered depth, the narrowest preview reports 30.07 per cent of the frame stopping inside the solid against 1.19 per cent that reaches an actual surface, with 68.58 per cent walking through everything and leaving; the widest preview gives 29.34, 3.36 and 67.02. What is on screen is that arithmetic: fragments and speckle where a whole lattice should be. The camera runs down the line x equals y equals 0.5, half a cell from the lumps in both screen axes, because the origin itself is inside one of them.

stages.title: Subtract a half
stages.body: One term fixes both faults. fract(p) minus 0.5 runs from minus a half to a half, so the sphere sits in the middle of its cell and no longer needs cutting up, and the value no longer jumps: crossing a wall swings the coordinate from just under a half to just over minus a half, which is a sign change in a quantity whose length is what matters. For a sphere the result is not an approximation, it is exact. On each axis the term is the distance to the nearest half-integer on that axis, and choosing the nearest independently on each axis is the same as choosing the nearest centre outright, so the sphere the field measures really is the closest one. The camera goes back on the axis, which passes 0.7071 from every centre and so keeps 0.4071 of clear space at all times. Counted as the camera passes a whole-numbered depth, ninety per cent of the frame lands on a surface — 89.99 at the narrowest preview, 89.87 at the widest — and 0.04 and 0.08 per cent respectively report nothing at all. That last figure is the escape channel down the axis, where every step is at least 0.4071 long and sixty-four of them carry the ray past 20: a speck at the dead centre of the frame, and a few dashes further out on the widest previews. The remaining tenth is neither. One row off the axis the clearance falls toward 0.2, the steps shorten to match, and a ray at p of 0.60 and 0.005 has spent all sixty-four of them by t of 19.345 — short of the far distance, so it comes back as a hit the caller cannot question. That is Module 8's warning about exhausted marches, arriving the first time a scene has no far side. The lattice repeats every unit in z and the camera covers 0.4 of a unit a second, so the whole view repeats exactly every 2.5 seconds.

stages.title: The cell's id
stages.body: floor(p) is the other half of what fract threw away: the whole-numbered part, which names the cell. It is constant everywhere inside that cell, so a number built from it is one number for the whole copy rather than something that varies across it, which is exactly what is needed to make copies differ without making any single copy wrong. Here it drives the radius, through a plain sine of a weighted sum of the three components — not a hash, so neighbouring cells are related rather than scattered. The three weights do not treat the axes alike, though. Along z, into the screen, the phase advances 51.57 degrees a cell and the radius swells and ebbs over a period of about seven cells; across x and y, which are the two axes the frame actually shows you, it advances 97.40 and 131.78 degrees a cell, so neighbours there read as alternation rather than as a swell. The radius runs 0.24 to 0.36, and the largest sphere holds 3.375 times the volume of the smallest. The cell whose id is 0, 0, 0 comes out at 0.3000, the one a step further along z at 0.3470 and the next at 0.3584, while the id minus 1, 0, 1 gives 0.2570 and the id 1, 0, 2 gives 0.2790. There is a price, and it shows. The field now reports the distance to this cell's sphere, and a neighbouring cell's may be both bigger and nearer, so the number can be too large and the ray can overstep. Counted at the same point in the cycle as the last stage, where not one pixel ended up inside a sphere, 2.53 per cent of the narrowest frame now does, and 2.91 per cent of the widest; the share that leaves the scene entirely rises from 0.04 per cent to 0.17 at the narrowest preview and from 0.08 to 0.11 at the widest. Surfaces still account for 88.36 and 88.32 per cent, with 8.94 and 8.66 per cent the exhausted marches down the channels the last stage described, so the lattice reads correctly — but it is no longer exact, and Module 11 is where that bill is itemised.

stages.title: Turn each copy in place
stages.body: A sphere is the wrong shape to rotate, so the copies are cubes. The order of the three lines is the whole idea: fract and the half give the coordinate inside the cell, Module 5's mat2 turns that coordinate about the cell's own centre, and only then does sdBox measure it. Rotating the coordinate rather than the shape is what keeps the field honest — a rotation preserves length, so distances measured in the turned frame are the distances in the unturned one, and nothing has to be divided back out. The angle mixes time with the cell id, so every copy turns at the same rate from a different starting point: at the moment the shader starts, the cell whose id is 0, 0, 0 is square-on, the one a step further along z stands at 40.11 degrees and the next at 80.21, while a step in x either way gives minus and plus 63.03. Size has to be checked against the cell rather than guessed. A half-extent of 0.22 puts the cube's furthest corner 0.3811 from its centre and the corner of its footprint in the turning plane at 0.3111, both inside the half-cell of 0.5, so no cube ever reaches into its neighbour at any angle. The census, taken at that same starting moment, holds up: 89.44 per cent of the narrowest frame lands on a surface and 88.72 per cent of the widest, with 10.13 and 10.76 per cent the exhausted marches down the channels again. The angle advances at 0.6 radians a second, and because a cube looks the same every quarter turn, each copy is back to an appearance it has already had every 2.618 seconds, while the camera crosses a cell every 2.5. Those two are not in any whole-number ratio, so the view never repeats.
